title: Sorting & Searching Algorithms
description: Six roads covering how classic sorting and searching algorithms actually behave -- their complexity, their guarantees, and where they break down.
learningObjectives: Compare average-case time complexity across common sorting algorithms
Explain why Binary Search requires a sorted input
Identify which sorting algorithms are stable
Explain why Binary Search is O(log n)

questions.description:
Most comparison-based sorting algorithms share the same theoretical floor for average-case performance on arbitrary input.

What is the best average-case time complexity any comparison-based sort can achieve?

options.label: A) O(n)
options.explanation: Incorrect. O(n) would mean sorting with a single pass over the data -- comparison sorts can't guarantee correctness with that few comparisons.

options.label: B) O(n log n)
options.explanation: Correct! Comparison-based sorting has a proven lower bound of O(n log n) -- algorithms like Merge Sort and Heapsort hit this bound.

options.label: C) O(n^2)
options.explanation: Incorrect. O(n^2) is what naive algorithms like Bubble Sort or Insertion Sort do in the average/worst case -- it's not the best achievable.

options.label: D) O(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sorting requires examining the elements at least once, so constant time is impossible for arbitrary input.

questions.description:
Binary Search repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the target to the middle element.

What must be true about the input array for Binary Search to work correctly?

options.label: A) The array must be sorted
options.explanation: Correct! Binary Search relies on ordering to decide which half to discard -- on an unsorted array, discarding half the data could discard the answer.

options.label: B) All elements must be unique
options.explanation: Incorrect. Duplicate values don't break Binary Search -- it will still find a match, just not necessarily a specific occurrence.

options.label: C) The array length must be even
options.explanation: Incorrect. Binary Search works fine on arrays of any length -- the midpoint calculation just rounds.

options.label: D) No precondition is needed
options.explanation: Incorrect. Without a sorted array, the halving logic has no basis for deciding which side the target is on.

questions.description:
A sorting algorithm is stable if elements that compare as equal keep their original relative order after sorting.

Which of these algorithms is naturally stable?

options.label: A) Merge Sort
options.explanation: Correct! Merge Sort's merge step takes from the left run first when values are equal, preserving original order -- it's stable by construction.

options.label: B) Quicksort
options.explanation: Incorrect. Quicksort's partitioning swaps elements across the array and typically does not preserve the relative order of equal elements.

options.label: C) Heapsort
options.explanation: Incorrect. Heapsort's heap-extraction process reorders equal elements based on heap structure, not their original positions.

options.label: D) Selection Sort
options.explanation: Incorrect. Selection Sort's swaps can move an equal element past another equal element, breaking their original order.

questions.description:
Quicksort's performance depends heavily on how balanced each partition is.

Which situation triggers Quicksort's O(n^2) worst case?

options.label: A) Repeatedly picking a pivot that's the smallest or largest remaining element
options.explanation: Correct! If every pivot lands at one end of the partition (e.g. always picking the first element on already-sorted data), each partition only shrinks by one, giving O(n^2).

options.label: B) Picking pivots uniformly at random
options.explanation: Incorrect. Random pivot selection makes the worst case extremely unlikely -- it's actually a standard defense against it.

options.label: C) Sorting an array with fewer than 10 elements
options.explanation: Incorrect. Array size alone doesn't trigger the worst case -- partition balance does.

options.label: D) Sorting an array with an even number of elements
options.explanation: Incorrect. Array length parity has no effect on Quicksort's partitioning behavior.

questions.description:
Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time in every case, including the worst case, unlike Quicksort.

What does Merge Sort typically trade away to get that guarantee?

options.label: A) It uses O(n) extra space for the merge step
options.explanation: Correct! The merge step needs auxiliary arrays to combine two sorted runs, so standard Merge Sort isn't in-place -- that's the price for its guaranteed O(n log n).

options.label: B) It sometimes produces an incorrectly sorted array
options.explanation: Incorrect. Merge Sort is always correct -- the tradeoff is memory, not correctness.

options.label: C) It skips comparisons to save time
options.explanation: Incorrect. Merge Sort still performs all necessary comparisons; it doesn't cut corners there.

options.label: D) It loses stability to save memory
options.explanation: Incorrect. Standard Merge Sort is stable -- it doesn't sacrifice stability for its time guarantee.

questions.description:
Each comparison in Binary Search eliminates half of the remaining candidates.

Why does that give Binary Search a time complexity of O(log n)?

options.label: A) Because the search space is halved each step, so it takes about log2(n) steps to shrink to one element
options.explanation: Correct! Repeatedly halving n until you reach 1 takes log2(n) steps -- that's exactly the definition of logarithmic time.

options.label: B) Because it checks every element once
options.explanation: Incorrect. Checking every element once describes O(n) linear search, not Binary Search's halving strategy.

options.label: C) Because it re-sorts the array on every call
options.explanation: Incorrect. Binary Search assumes the array is already sorted -- it doesn't re-sort, which is exactly what keeps it fast.

options.label: D) Because it always finds the target in one comparison
options.explanation: Incorrect. Only the middle element is checked first; most searches take multiple halving steps, not just one.
